summary:
Montserrat stands under the United Kingdom's framework as a British Overseas Territory and must comply with international human rights instruments, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Domestically, Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. 'Discriminatory' is defined as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful in Montserrat since 2001. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for everyone, and the age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity, so a visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex faces an age of consent of 18 rather than 16.

Relationship recognition does not extend to same-sex couples. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal in Montserrat, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family.

Organised LGBT social infrastructure is close to absent. Montserrat has no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues. Several hotels on the island welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment. A 2012 account by GlobalGayz describes gay life as barely existing locally and the social scene as decimated.
tangentialFactors:
Montserrat's prohibitions were swept away as part of a single British decision to scrap anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories, including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, on the stated ground that the laws violated signed international human rights agreements. The Associated Press reported the decision in January 2001.

The reform was imposed from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent, and was framed locally as a cultural rift with the United Kingdom. That recorded opposition is the clearest available signal of the official and religious climate a visitor may encounter alongside the constitutional protections.

A 1989 hurricane and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption reshaped the 104 km2 island, wastelanding the south and displacing over half the population north. The resulting sparse and dispersed settlement pattern is part of the context for the thin social scene documented by travel sources.
localsOnly:
For residents, Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code are the operative non-discrimination provisions, with the Labour Code covering employment treatment and the constitutional article reaching discrimination more broadly on grounds including sexual orientation.

Residual criminal exposure shapes private life for residents as well as visitors: group sex and sex in public are offences for everyone, and the age of consent of 18 for homosexual activity against 16 for heterosexual activity means conduct lawful between opposite-sex partners of the same age can be an offence between partners read locally as same-sex.

Residents have no route to legal recognition of a same-sex relationship. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Article 10(1) of the Constitution secures the right to marry only a person of the opposite sex.

The decriminalisation was carried out by an order imposed from London over the objections of local politicians and religious leaders rather than with their consent, and was framed locally as a cultural rift. Residents live with that recorded opposition alongside the formal protections, and the island offers no dedicated LGBT venues, only hotels with non-discrimination policies.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents violence, harassment or hate-crime incidents targeting trans people in Montserrat, and none records how the residual offences of group sex and public sex are actually enforced. Enforcement practice is unresolved.

Gender recognition, legal gender markers on passports or local identity documents, entry or immigration screening of trans travellers, and access to gender-affirming healthcare in Montserrat are not sourced. Nothing in the inventory addresses whether a trans visitor's documents or presentation trigger secondary examination or outing.

The description of the island's social scene rests on a 2012 GlobalGayz travel account and a tertiary encyclopaedia entry; its currency is unresolved. The Associated Press report on the five-territory reform dates from January 2001.

Constitutional Articles 10(1) and 16 and Article 79 of the Labour Code are quoted here from secondary sources. Verification against the primary instruments is unresolved.
